system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2163-04-09 20:00:00 to 2163-04-11 14:20:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 52-year-old female with systemic lupus erythematosus and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis was admitted for one week of right shoulder pain and low-grade fever. Imaging showed changes consistent with early avascular necrosis, and joint aspiration revealed elevated white blood cells with no crystals, raising concern for septic arthritis despite negative cultures. She was started on IV vancomycin, with significant improvement in pain and function. Blood and fluid cultures remained negative, and lupus serologies were stable, supporting infection over flare. She was discharged home on a two-week course of vancomycin administered with dialysis and a single dose of fluconazole for a concurrent yeast infection. Follow-up was arranged with primary care, rheumatology, and orthopedics.
problems: Aseptic necrosis of head of humerus

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having fevers since my fistula surgery a couple days ago. I felt really tired and had one episode of vomiting at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you had a fistula revision recently? When was that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just two days ago. They gave me linezolid before the surgery because of my history with resistant bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. You went to dialysis yesterday and they noticed you had a fever then too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was 100.3°F. But the nurse said my fistula looked clean—no redness or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We checked your labs in the ER. Your white count is normal, but your liver enzymes are elevated—ALT and AST are high, and your alkaline phosphatase is 398.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Is that from the antibiotics? I’m still on Keflex for that groin rash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s one possibility. It could also be related to a mild viral illness or even lupus activity. But your CRP and ESR are high, which suggests inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had these liver enzyme flares before. But the fever is new. Could it be from the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Transient bacteremia after a procedure can cause a short fever. But we drew blood cultures to be safe. You also got one dose of vancomycin in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to vancomycin though—listed in my chart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I saw that. The team wasn’t sure what the allergy was—no red man syndrome or anaphylaxis noted. But we won’t repeat it unless absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I’ve also been more short of breath lately—only walk a block before needing to rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that in your history. Your chest X-ray shows no pneumonia or fluid in the lungs. Heart size is a bit enlarged, but no acute issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it my heart? I’ve had normal stress tests before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EKG is stable, and troponin is only slightly elevated but not in the range for a heart attack. Given your history of diastolic dysfunction, we’ve ordered an exercise stress test to check for ischemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my right-sided belly pain—it’s been there for years, but it’s still tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. You’re scheduled for an ultrasound tomorrow morning to check your liver and bile ducts since your liver tests are up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your ultrasound is back. Your liver looks normal, but there’s a 1 cm dilation in the common bile duct.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I’ve had ultrasounds before—was it there last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It wasn’t seen on one prior study, but it was noted before. Since it’s been intermittent and your liver enzymes are already coming down, we don’t think it’s urgent. But you should follow up with GI and get an MRCP as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. Any sign of infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures are still pending, but so far no growth. You haven’t had a fever since yesterday morning—your highest was 99.1 last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it might just be a reaction to the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely. No local signs of infection, and you’re feeling better. We’ll keep monitoring, but we don’t plan to restart antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I had dialysis this morning. Everything went fine. Fistula still feels strong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your labs this morning show your liver enzymes are already improving—ALT down to 148, AST to 90. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Should I stop Keflex when I finish the course?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, finish the full course. Your folliculitis is improving, and stopping early could lead to resistance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I just reviewed your case. You’ve been afebrile for over 24 hours, no new symptoms, and labs are trending better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning. Blood cultures will still be pending, but the risk is low at this point.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the shortness of breath and the bile duct issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to follow up with your cardiologist. The stress test is ordered—call their office to schedule. And please see a gastroenterologist about the bile duct finding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my regular meds—am I going back on all of them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home medications are continued. No changes—just keep up with dialysis and your usual routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your discharge orders are in. You’re free to go once we go over the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad I’m back to my baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send a summary to your PCP. Remember: follow up with your primary doctor, cardiologist, and gastroenterologist. Call if you develop fever again or any new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and stay well.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 52-year-old female with systemic lupus erythematosus and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis was admitted for fevers following a recent AV fistula revision. She developed postoperative fatigue, vomiting, and fever, prompting evaluation. Initial labs showed elevated inflammatory markers and transaminitis. Blood cultures were negative to date, and she remained afebrile after 24 hours without antibiotics. Her symptoms were attributed to likely transient bacteremia or viral illness. She also reported worsening exertional shortness of breath; chest imaging showed no acute process, and a stress test was ordered. Abdominal ultrasound revealed 1 cm common bile duct dilation, previously noted intermittently, with plans for outpatient MRCP. She improved clinically, returned to baseline, and was discharged home with follow-up arranged in primary care, cardiology, and gastroenterology.
